k1401: Commuting already happens. The SH2 highway takes 30–60 minutes depending on traffic, and 41 buses a day run between the two cities. Renting in Tirana costs about 57% more than in Durrës, so the gap that makes Durrës attractive to people working in Tirana is already there. The train shortens the trip and makes it predictable, which is what turns an occasional commute into a daily one.
k1402: What is already in the price
k1403: Our rule for infrastructure is simple. A project that already works is fully in the price. A project that is financed and under construction is about half priced in. An announcement without money should not be bought at all. The railway sits in the middle category: its main upside is still ahead and comes when trains physically run, not when the next deadline is announced.
k1405: It won't lift the whole city. Durrës lost about 21,000 residents between the 2011 and 2023 censuses — its population was 153,614 in 2023 — so local demand is not growing on its own. Any gain will be concentrated where the train changes daily life: within walking distance of the stations along the Tirana–Durrës corridor, including inland districts such as Shkozet, and in the parts of Plazh and Golem that commuters could live in year-round. One market forecast puts that gain at 5–10% a year for homes near stations after launch — a medium-confidence estimate we would not build a purchase around.
k1406: It also won't fix what the seaside zones struggle with — the season, the sewerage in Golem, the older stock on the beach strip.
k1407: How to use this as a buyer
k1408: Buy for the use you have today, and treat the train as upside rather than as the reason.
k1409: If commuting to Tirana is the plan, check the walking distance to a station, not the distance to the sea.
k1410: Don't pay a premium a seller justifies with "when the train opens" — ask which year they mean.
